# A scalar-centroid correction for the vertex sides of simplex sections

This is a one-sided statement about vertex-isolating centroidal sections.
It does not prove the same correction works for complementary caps or
for other simplex section types, and does not prove the general weighted
stationary-section theorem.

Let d≥2, let T be a d-dimensional simplex, and let y have positive
barycentric coordinates λ_0,...,λ_d, all at most1/d. Translate y to0,
and let g be the ordinary centroid of the translated T. Write
γ=(d/(d+1))^d. For each vertex i there is a unique section through0,
with section centroid0, separating vertex i from the other vertices.
If λ_j=1/d, the plane may contain a simplex vertex, which does not affect
its section area or cap volume.

Orient the unit normal u_i toward vertex i. Define p_i to be its cap
volume fraction and s_i=S_i(u_i·g)/|T|, where S_i is its section area.
Then there is an explicit c>0 such that

    p_i−c s_i ≥ γ                    for every i.       (1)

Choose two distinct indices attaining a=min λ_i and b=max λ_i. If all
coordinates coincide, any two distinct indices can be chosen. Put

    E = d(d+1) − Σ_{j remaining} 1/λ_j,
    c = (d+1)/E.                                      (2)

Here “remaining” omits the chosen minimum and maximum indices.

## Proof

The vertex-i section has edge intercept fractions dλ_j for j≠i, so

    p_i = d^d Π_{j≠i} λ_j.

A raw cap margin is d−Σ_{j≠i} ξ_j/λ_j, where ξ denotes the barycentric
coordinates on T. Its section coarea factor divided by |T| equals p_i:
shifting its threshold is a homothety of a cone of margin d. Therefore

    s_i = p_i [d−(1/(d+1))Σ_{j≠i}1/λ_j].               (3)

This also follows directly by differentiating the displayed cap product.
Set P=d^d Π_jλ_j, t_i=1/λ_i, and

    T_0=Σ_jt_j−d(d+1).

Then p_i=P t_i and s_i=P t_i(t_i−T_0)/(d+1). Since
E=1/a+1/b−T_0, substitution of (2) gives

    p_i−c s_i = (P/E)t_i(1/a+1/b−t_i).                (4)

First E is positive. Put r_j=1−dλ_j. These numbers are nonnegative
and sum to1. Let A be their largest value and B their smallest, at the
two omitted indices. Since all λ_j>0, A<1. The remaining r_j obey

    Σ_remaining r_j/(1−r_j)
        ≤ (Σ_remaining r_j)/(1−A)
        = (1−A−B)/(1−A) ≤1.

Consequently

    E/d = d+1−Σ_remaining 1/(1−r_j)
        = 2−Σ_remaining r_j/(1−r_j) ≥1.              (5)

The quadratic in (4) is concave on t_i∈[1/b,1/a]. Its two endpoint
values agree. Thus (4) is at least

    R = P/(Eab) = d^d Π_remaining λ_j / E.

Let x_j=1/(dλ_j) for the d−1 remaining indices and D=E/d. Then
x_j>0, D>0, and Σ_remaining x_j+D=d+1. Moreover

    R = 1/(D Π_remaining x_j).

The arithmetic–geometric mean inequality for these d positive numbers
shows DΠx_j≤((d+1)/d)^d, proving (1).

The argument includes repeated extrema and λ_j=1/d. At uniform
λ_j=1/(d+1), E=d+1, c=1, and (1) is equality for every vertex cap.
More generally, if all remaining λ_j equal1/(d+1), the two extremal
vertex caps attain equality in (1).

## Exact limits of this result

For a complementary cap, the corrected fraction is 1−(p_i−c s_i).
Controlling it by γ requires the additional upper bound
p_i−c s_i≤1−γ, which is not proved above. The script
`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/simplex-explicit-scalar-correction-check.py` found no failure in its
finite exact samples, but these checks do not supply that missing proof.
For quadrilateral tetrahedral sections and for a general convex body,
the quadratic expression (4) is unavailable.
